claims.claim: Earth's Moon orbits at an average distance of about 384,400 kilometers (238,855 miles), with a radius of about 1,740 kilometers, less than a third of Earth's width.

The leading hypothesis for the Moon's formation is the giant-impact hypothesis: a Mars-sized body (named Theia) collided with the young Earth and debris from the collision accumulated to form the Moon.

Apollo missions returned about 382 kilograms (842 pounds) of lunar samples; the rocks' ages, melted early history, and composition matching Earth's (including oxygen isotopes) point to the Moon forming from a large impact roughly 60 million years after the solar system began.

The Moon's bright highlands are ancient, heavily cratered crust, while the dark, relatively smooth maria are impact basins filled with lava between about 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago; craters have been preserved for billions of years because the Moon has no wind or flowing water.

The Moon's gravitational pull plays a major role in driving Earth's ocean tides, and the Moon's orbit produces the monthly cycle of lunar phases, which takes about 29 days from one new moon to the next.
The Moon rotates once per orbit (synchronous rotation), so the same hemisphere always faces Earth; the far side is not always dark, just never visible from Earth.

Moons (natural satellites) are naturally formed bodies that orbit planets; the solar system has hundreds of known moons, with NASA's catalog listing 891 confirmed moons as of March 25, 2025, and counts continuing to grow as discoveries are confirmed.

Jupiter's four largest moons are the Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610; Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system (larger than Mercury), Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system, Callisto is an ancient heavily cratered world, and Europa's icy crust is thought to hide a liquid-water ocean.

Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon in the solar system known to have a substantial atmosphere, with clouds, rain, rivers, lakes, and seas of liquid hydrocarbons such as methane and ethane.

Enceladus is a small icy moon of Saturn with geyser-like jets that spray water vapor and ice particles from a subsurface liquid-water ocean into space, discovered by NASA's Cassini spacecraft in 2005.
Giant-planet moon counts are documented but change over time; for example, Jupiter had 115 moons officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union as of August 2026.

Moons matter for understanding the solar system because they are small worlds that preserve impact and formation history, and several icy moons may hold liquid-water oceans beneath their crusts, making them priority targets in the search for life beyond Earth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The rate at which the Moon is receding from Earth differs slightly between two NASA pages: Moon Facts says 'about an inch farther away each year' while Moon Formation says 'about an inch and a half per year' (measured with Apollo surface reflectors).
positions: NASA Moon Facts: about 1 inch per year
NASA Moon Formation: about 1.5 inches per year
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states 'roughly an inch and a half per year' and cites only the Moon Formation page, which gives the more specific Apollo reflector measurement. The discrepancy is a rounding difference between pages, not a scientific disagreement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Moon counts differ across dates and pages: 891 confirmed moons total (March 25, 2025) on the moons index, versus 115 IAU-recognized moons of Jupiter alone (August 2026) on the Jupiter moons page.
positions: 891 confirmed moons as of March 25, 2025 (index page)
Jupiter: 115 IAU-recognized moons as of August 2026
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both figures are reported in the lesson, each with its as-of date, and the lesson explains that counts keep changing as new moons are confirmed. No single 'final' count is asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Status of the Moon's origin: NASA presents the giant-impact scenario as the leading explanation ('thought to have formed in a tremendous collision') while noting models are still refined and older theories (capture, co-accretion) fell out of favor after Apollo.
positions: Giant impact of a Mars-sized body (leading hypothesis per NASA)
Older hypotheses: gravitational capture or co-accretion with Earth
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the giant-impact hypothesis as NASA's leading explanation, not as a settled certainty, and notes that computer models are still being refined. This matches NASA's own framing.

sourceRecords.title: How Did the Moon Form?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NASA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user agent. Supports: the giant-impact hypothesis as the leading explanation - a Mars-sized object named Theia smashed into the young Earth and flung molten and vaporized debris into orbit that became the Moon; Apollo missions returning 842 pounds (382 kilograms) of lunar samples; the Moon forming about 60 million years after the solar system began; a magma-ocean early Moon; oxygen-isotope matches between lunar and Earth rocks; older capture and co-accretion ideas falling out of favor; lunar surface reflectors showing the Moon recedes about an inch and a half per year; models still being refined. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Moon Facts

Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Moons of Jupiter
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NASA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user agent. Supports: Jupiter has 115 moons officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union as of August 2026, with the number not capturing the complexity of the Jovian system; the Galilean satellites discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 (Simon Marius observed them around the same time; the names Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto came from Marius's 1614 list); Ganymede as Jupiter's largest moon and the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury and Pluto; Callisto as Jupiter's second largest and the solar system's third largest moon; Io as the most volcanically active world in the solar system; Europa as about 90% the size of Earth's Moon. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
